newsitem.title: ITALY: Two children among 10 Italians kidnapped in Yemen.
newsitem.headline: Two children among 10 Italians kidnapped in Yemen.

text.p: Ten Italian tourists, including the brother of a former senator and two children aged nine and 10, have been abducted in two incidents in Yemen, the Italian Foreign Ministry said on Thursday.

A ministry official said six people were kidnapped in the south of the country on Wednesday afternoon while on their way to Al Mukallaa on the Gulf of Aden coast. They had been taken to the interior of the country.
A further four Italians were abducted near Khamir, some 100 km (60 miles) north of the capital Sanaa, on Thursday morning.
The group of six consisted of two families of three from the southern Italian city of Naples.
One of those captured was Enrico De Notaris, brother of former Italian parliamentarian Francesco De Notaris.
Francesco said his brother had managed to telephone him from Yemen after the abduction and, finding no one home, had left a message on an answering machine.

"My dear Francesco," Enrico said in the message. "I've been taken prisoner by a group in Yemen. Please let everyone know we're being treated well... I think we've been kidnapped as part of an economic claim."
Francesco De Notaris said he had talked to his brother just before the party left for the Arabian peninsula on Tuesday about a spate of recent abductions involving Italian tourists.
"He asked me if it was true another Italian had been kidnapped but he didn't seem worried," Francesco recalled.

Enrico De Notaris' nine-year-old son, Svevo, was also among the hostages along with a 10-year-old girl, Francesca Ferraro. The other three victims were identified as Adolfo Ferraro, Ida Genovese and Mariella Plumbo.
Nothing further was known about the four tourists abducted in Thursday's incident.
The kidnappings were the latest in a series carried out by Yemeni tribesmen in one of the Arab world's poorest countries.

An Italian kidnapped earlier this month was released last Sunday and two others who were abducted in late July were freed after one day. In March, 11 Germans including seven motorcycle tourists were abducted and later freed.

The tribesmen have tried to use hostages -- who have included French and U.S. diplomats and a Saudi ambassador -- as bargaining chips in land and water disputes with the government and foreign oil firms.
All hostages have so far been released unharmed. Giorgio Gonanomi, the Italian released last Sunday, said he had been fed exotic fruits and treated wonderfully during his five days in captivity.
